subtopics.title: The six heading levels (h1–h6)
subtopics.explanation: HTML provides six heading levels, h1 (most important) through h6 (least). They label sections of content and convey importance and nesting — not size. h1 is the page's main title; h2s are its top-level sections; h3s sit under an h2, and so on. The browser styles them with decreasing default size, but that's cosmetic — the meaning is the hierarchy.

subtopics.title: The document outline (one h1, no skipped levels)
subtopics.explanation: Headings build the page's outline, like a table of contents. Use exactly one h1 for the page's main subject, then descend logically — h2 under h1, h3 under h2 — without skipping levels (don't jump h2 → h4). Assistive tech, search engines, and 'jump to heading' features all rely on this hierarchy to convey structure.

subtopics.title: Whitespace collapsing
subtopics.explanation: By default, HTML collapses any run of spaces, tabs, and newlines in your source into a single space when rendered. So '   hello\n\nworld   ' shows as 'hello world'. This lets you indent and wrap source code freely without affecting output. To preserve exact whitespace, use a <pre> element or the CSS white-space property.

foundations.overview:
Headings and paragraphs are the first elements every HTML author learns, but using them well is about structure, not appearance. Headings (h1–h6) create a hierarchical outline of the page; paragraphs (

) group running text. The browser handles spacing and whitespace collapsing for you, so the author's job is to choose elements for what the content *is*, not how big it should look.

foundations.whyItMatters: Headings define the document outline that screen readers and search engines use to navigate and understand a page; paragraphs make prose readable and machine-parseable. Getting the hierarchy right is a baseline accessibility and SEO requirement and a common beginner interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a page like a book: the title is the h1, chapters are h2s, sections within a chapter are h3s, and so on. Paragraphs are the sentences of prose between them. You'd never label a minor section 'Chapter 1' just because you wanted bigger text — likewise, never pick a heading level for its size.
foundations.browserPerspective:
The browser parses headings into the accessibility tree with a 'heading' role and a level (1–6), which screen readers expose for navigation. It also collapses source whitespace into single spaces during parsing and adds default top/bottom margins to

and heading elements via the user-agent stylesheet.
foundations.realWorldUsage:
Every article, blog post, documentation page, and landing page uses headings to chunk content and paragraphs for prose. Addresses and poems use

foundations.businessImpact: A clear heading outline improves SEO ranking and the chance of rich results, and meets accessibility requirements (WCAG) that reduce legal risk and widen your audience — both directly affect reach.
foundations.engineeringImpact:
A logical heading structure makes content self-documenting and easy to style and restyle with CSS. Relying on the browser's whitespace collapsing and default margins keeps markup clean and free of hacks like

foundations.performanceImpact:

commonMisconceptions.myth: You pick a heading level based on how big you want the text.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Heading levels convey structure and importance, not size. Choose the level that fits the outline and use CSS to control the visual size.

visualExplorer.title: Building a document outline

config.intro: A well-structured page reads like a table of contents. Follow these steps to build a clean heading outline.

steps.name: One h1 for the page
steps.detail: Give the page a single h1 describing its main subject — the title at the top of the outline.

steps.name: h2 for top sections
steps.detail: Each major section of the page gets an h2, sitting directly under the h1 in the outline.

steps.name: h3 nested under h2
steps.detail: Subsections of an h2 use h3. Never jump from h2 straight to h4 — that skips a level.

steps.name: Paragraphs fill the sections
steps.detail:
Within each section, write running text as

elements, one idea per paragraph.

steps.name: Style with CSS, not levels
steps.detail: If an h3 needs to look bigger, set its font-size in CSS — don't promote it to an h2.

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: There should be one h1 (the page's subject). 'Installation' is a section, so it belongs at h2, and 'Troubleshooting' sits under it as an h3 — jumping to h4 skips the h2/h3 levels and breaks the outline. Heading levels reflect structure, not visual preference.

theory.question: What are the HTML heading elements and how should you choose which level to use?
theory.directAnswer: HTML has six heading levels, h1 (highest) through h6 (lowest). You choose a level by its place in the document's structure, not by how big you want the text. Use one h1 for the page's main subject, then descend logically — h2 for sections, h3 for subsections — without skipping levels. Visual size is controlled with CSS.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: h1–h6 are section-heading elements that express importance and nesting, building the page's outline.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Documents need a hierarchical structure that humans and machines (screen readers, search engines) can navigate; heading ranks encode that hierarchy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser assigns each heading a 'heading' role and a level in the accessibility tree, and assistive tech lets users jump between headings by level.

theory.whyImportant: A correct heading outline is a baseline accessibility (WCAG) and SEO requirement and a classic beginner interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: On a docs page, the title is the h1, 'Installation' and 'Usage' are h2s, and 'Troubleshooting' under Installation is an h3 — letting a screen-reader user jump section to section.

nestedTopics.title: One h1 per page
nestedTopics.explanation: Conventionally a page has a single h1 describing its main subject.

nestedTopics.title: No skipped levels
nestedTopics.explanation: Don't jump h2 → h4; descend one level at a time so the outline has no gaps.

nestedTopics.title: Structure not size
nestedTopics.explanation: Pick a level for its meaning in the hierarchy; use CSS to change how big it looks.

followUps.question: Why is it bad to choose a heading by its font size?
followUps.answer: It corrupts the document outline that assistive tech and crawlers rely on. Two headings that look the same size but mean different things should differ by CSS, not by misusing levels.

followUps.question: How do you make an h3 look as large as an h1?
followUps.answer: Set its font-size in CSS. The heading level stays correct for the outline while the appearance changes independently.

elements, and rebuild the outline so there's one h1, then h2/h3 descending without skips. If a heading needs to look a certain size, set that in CSS rather than changing its level.

productionDeepDive.architecture:
Define a consistent content structure across the site: one h1 per page (often the page title), h2 for top-level sections, h3+ for subsections, and prose in

. Templates and CMS field rules should enforce this so authors can't accidentally skip levels.
productionDeepDive.performance:
Headings and paragraphs are cheap. The win is avoiding bloat: spacing hacks like stacked
s and empty

s grow the DOM and complicate styling; clean structural markup keeps the tree small.
productionDeepDive.security: Markup itself isn't a security boundary, but content rendered from user input (comments, CMS) must be escaped or sanitized to prevent XSS — headings and paragraphs are common injection points in rich-text editors.
productionDeepDive.scaling: In component libraries, expose a heading primitive that takes a level prop so nested components render the correct level for their context, keeping a single coherent outline across deeply nested pages.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A logical heading outline is self-documenting and trivial to restyle, since visual size lives entirely in CSS. Avoiding presentational hacks means the markup reads like the content's structure.
productionDeepDive.observability: Automated tools (axe, Lighthouse, pa11y) detect skipped heading levels and missing/duplicate h1s in CI; manual screen-reader passes confirm the outline reads logically for key pages.

caseStudies.problem: Auto-generated docs pages produced inconsistent or skipped heading levels, breaking the page outline and in-page navigation.
caseStudies.solution: A heading component that computes the correct level from nesting depth, plus CI checks for a single h1 and no skipped levels.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more abstraction in the rendering layer versus a guaranteed-correct outline.
caseStudies.lessons: Encoding the outline rules in tooling beats relying on every author to remember them.
